turns.player_line: I find Old Maren by the chapel steps and ask her about the blackened fields.
turns.narration:
You leave the hearth's warmth behind and cross the square to the chapel steps. Old Maren is where she's always been — seated with her basket set a step out of reach, the way it's always set. She looks up, eyes sharp as a crow's, and takes in the torch in your hand without flinching.

"Black at the root," she says, nodding slowly at your question. "Ain't rot. Rot comes up out of the earth. This comes down from above." Her voice drops, dry as the dead field itself. "The last king — the one they laid in the crypt under this very ground — he died mid-crowning. The crown sat on his brow when the shadow took him, and it's been gnawing at your grain ever since. Three nights now, and it's hungry again."

She leans in, then stops herself, her gaze drifting to the rim of her basket. "I know what can unmake the thing. I've always known." She taps a knuckle against the wicker, once, twice. "But I don't give it away for nothing, child. You've seen where my basket sits. You know what it takes to close the distance."

The want in her eyes is plain and old: bread. The real kind, warm, with the crust still on it.

What will you do — find her a loaf and earn the name she's holding, press her some other way, or step back and let her keep it?

You leave the mayor's hall without another word — Aldous's chair scrapes as he follows you to the door, then the room's cold takes him back. The square is quiet under the lanterns, and the chapel door stands ajar.

Father Cael is on the steps before you reach them, hands shaking so hard the words come out blurred. "Hold still," he murmurs, and presses his palms to your brow a breath's length. "The dark keeps off where the blessing is. I don't know what else it is. I know only that." His eyes catch the white candle in your hand and go very wide — then away again, before he can ask.

The undercroft door breathes cold. You go down, torch in one hand, the unburnt candle warm in the other. The stairs are older than the chapel, and the torchlight stops at the wall and stays there, the dark beyond it not merely unlit but *attentive*. The blessing thins as you descend, a held breath you can feel going thin at the back of your neck.

At the bottom, someone is breathing. Grave-digger Sable crouches in a shaft of nothing, trowel in his fist, and does not look at you when your light finds him. "I opened the door for him," he says, to the floor, three nights ago. "Three nights ago."

The candle in your hand is warm as a living thing. The torch sputters in the dark that is leaning in.

What do you light — keep the torch as your only light, or strike a spark to the candle of Vell?

turns.player_line: I talk to Sable, the grave-digger.
turns.narration:
You crouch down to his level in the shaft of nothing, and Sable's eyes still won't find yours — they track the floor like it's the only honest thing left. His trowel knocks once against stone, and he starts again, the words coming out in a broken order.

"I opened the door," he says, to the floor. "Three nights ago. He had the hall's seal in his hand, and he never raised his voice. Never raised his voice. I told myself it was a priest's errand, and I meant it, and I don't mean it now." His heavy hands work the trowel until the soil is a fine grey dust. "I can't sleep. I can't eat. The dark's been in my eyes since, and it won't let go."

The torch sputters again, and the dark leans in a half-step closer to both of you. Sable flinches without looking up. "Whatever you're down here for — I'll tell you the rest. I just... I need it to stop counting me as a hand that opened that door." His voice cracks on the last word.

The candle of Vell sits unburnt in your other hand, warm as a living thing, while the torch gutters. What will you do — promise him the forgiveness he's begging for, ask him plainly what the stranger did on the stairs, or strike a spark to the candle and let his eyes meet yours in its light?

turns.player_line: I confront the thing guarding the altar.
turns.narration:
You go past Sable without a word — he doesn't stop you, and the torchlight finds the altar, and what stands before it finds you in the same breath. A shape of cold that was a man once, and it does not speak.

You act first. Your blade slips out of its line and passes wide through the cold air — a fumble even you can feel in the wrist. The wight answers with a hand like a frozen branch, and it too finds nothing but air.

Then you find the mark. The edge bites in, and the shape shudders as cold water shudders. Its reach finds no purchase on you. Again the blade takes flesh of cold, and again its hand swings through empty air. Once more it stumbles on the stone itself, the blow a fumble that misses clean.

The last strike drives home, and the shape goes slack. The cold floods out of it like a long breath, and it drops to the flagstones, unconscious — not gone. Not yet. You are whole, not a scratch on you, and the night's work earns you 50 XP.

The torchlight steadies. On the altar, the black iron circlet waits, and the shadow under it moves like something breathing. And in the dark beyond your light, a tall figure in a prophet's grey has been watching the whole time. His voice is soft, and every word is true: "The guardian was faithful. You are the first to pass it. The crown is unguarded now."

What will you do — take the crown from the altar, light the candle of Vell and let it show you what the dark is hiding, or step into the light and ask the prophet what he is?

turns.player_line: I face Vesper at the altar.
turns.narration:
You stand where you woke, the candle's small flame steady in your grip, and look the prophet in the face. He steps into its light, unhurried, and the shadow under the crown on the altar draws back a half-inch from the glow — the only thing in this room that flinches.

"You ask what I am," he says, softly. "I was the prophet of the crown, before the last king. I wore its name, and it wore me, and when the crown fell mid-crowning I fell with it. I came back for what was mine." He does not raise his voice. Every word is plain, and none of it is dressed up. "At the harvest moon's peak the crown is to be set again on the brow of Aldric the Last. When it is crowned, the blight is permanent. I tell you this because I do not lie, not because I wish you well."

His face is a candle seen through smoke. "You hold the only flame that can unmake it. I have not touched it, and I will not take it. I wait. That is all I am, here."

The wight lies dead a step off the flagstones. The crown sits unguarded on the altar, breathing in the dark. Three nights to the moon's peak.

What will you do — set the candle's flame against the black iron circlet now, press Vesper on why he never lies, or speak to Sable and take the stairs while you still can?
